title: Ofgem on windless winter weeks: how safe is Britain's power supply?
label: 28 October 2026 · Ofgem on Dunkelflaute and storage
summary: Peers questioned Peter Bingham, Ofgem's engineering director, about what happens when Britain goes days with little wind or sun. He said the risk is planned for, but couldn't say how rare an emergency the system is built to survive. On storage that lasts for days, the answer kept coming back to a national energy plan that isn't finished. He called the undersea cables to other countries reliable but not infallible, and said the real bottleneck is building the grid.

speakers.label: Peter Bingham
speakers.name: Peter Bingham
speakers.role: Director for Engineering and Technology, Ofgem

glossary.definition: German for 'dark doldrums': a spell of days or weeks with little wind and little sun, so wind farms and solar panels produce almost nothing.
The National Energy System Operator, the public body that balances Britain's electricity supply and demand minute by minute and plans for future needs.
A measure of energy. One gigawatt hour is roughly what 130,000 homes use in a day.

chapters.title: How rare a blackout are we planning for?
chapters.takeaway: Unlike gas, electricity has no 'once in so many years' standard, and Lord Ashcombe struggled to get a clear answer on how bad things are allowed to get.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: Britain is getting more and more of its power from wind and sun. How big a risk is that to keeping the lights on?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: We know it's a real issue. Wind and solar come and go, so you need other power stations you can switch on to fill the gaps, and that takes careful planning.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: The gas network is built to survive the kind of winter you'd expect once every 20 years. Is there anything like that for electricity?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: No. For electricity, the government's target is that supply shouldn't fall short of demand for more than three hours a year, on average. There isn't a 'once in so many years' measure.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: About a tenth of our power comes through cables from Europe. If Europe needs its own power just as we hit a long calm, dark spell, what odds are you planning for?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: NESO, which runs the grid, tests the system against tens of thousands of combinations of weather, breakdowns and conditions in Europe. The aim is to have enough supply in nearly all of them.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: You're still not giving me the answer I'm after. What chance of the system really struggling are they prepared to accept?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: It's statistical. You try to make sure the power available covers how high demand might go in almost every case. Past a certain point it's judged not worth the money to cover the last few. That said, we've recently bought more backup capacity than the standard requires.

chapters.title: Have the grid's safety rules been loosened?
chapters.takeaway: Lord Redwood asked about recent changes to the grid's technical safety rules, and Ofgem agreed to write with details.

turns.speaker: Lord Redwood
turns.text: NESO has recently relaxed some of the technical limits it uses to run the grid safely, presumably to fit in more renewables. Has that made the system riskier?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: I don't know the specific changes you mean. We did recently approve one that slightly widens the range of voltage allowed on part of the high-voltage network, to give NESO more room to manoeuvre within safe limits.

turns.speaker: Lord Redwood
turns.text: Could you write to us about all the changes to these standards over the past year?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Yes, of course.

chapters.title: Storage that lasts for days
chapters.takeaway: Peers pressed Ofgem on how Britain will store enough power to get through long calm spells, and were told much depends on a national plan that's still being written.

turns.speaker: Lord Krebs
turns.text: To get through a Dunkelflaute we'd need storage that runs for 100 hours or more. Your new support scheme seems aimed at much shorter storage. Why?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: It asked for at least eight hours and set no upper limit. The projects we've provisionally picked go up to 30 hours. I do think there's a case for much longer storage, and we'll consult on opening a future round to it.

turns.speaker: Lord Krebs
turns.text: That sounds rather like 'watch this space'.

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: This was the first round, and we'll learn a lot from it. We do plan to consult on what comes next.

turns.speaker: Lord Krebs
turns.text: Britain has about 24 gigawatt hours of long-duration storage, and uses around 700 a day. How much would we need to last ten days?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: The government's national energy plan should answer that. Storage is one option alongside gas, hydrogen, cables to other countries and paying big users to cut back. We'll definitely have times with more wind and solar power than we need, and it would be great to store that instead of burning gas later. Turning the plan into real projects is then a job for government.

turns.speaker: Lord Krebs
turns.text: So the answer is: there are lots of options, we're thinking about it, and we'll tell you next year.

turns.speaker: Earl Russell
turns.text: The longer you want to store energy for, the harder it gets. Does this need fresh thinking across government?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Absolutely. Storage on that scale, like hydrogen or pumping water uphill, needs huge investment, and batteries don't last long enough yet. Government once kept a separate support pot for very new technologies like tidal power. Something similar could help here.

turns.speaker: Baroness Whitaker
turns.text: How will you make sure this investment is good value for bill-payers?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: NESO is setting out possible routes that balance cost, security and cutting carbon. As the regulator, we want the Energy Secretary to pick the one that's cheapest for consumers.

turns.speaker: Baroness Whitaker
turns.text: Almost everyone who's given us evidence says the current markets don't work for long-duration storage. Do you agree?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Our scheme exists precisely because there are obstacles to getting that investment. It's a first attempt to get past them, and there's more to do.

turns.speaker: Baroness Whitaker
turns.text: When will we see the results of your first round?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: This year. We'll write and confirm the date.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Hydrogen and heat storage could last 100 hours or more. Why were none of them chosen?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: I'd need to check, but I don't think any were. The first round only accepted well-proven technologies, so newer ones were effectively shut out.

chapters.title: Relying on cables from abroad
chapters.takeaway: Ofgem says the undersea cables to other countries are reliable and aren't fully counted on in planning, but accepts they aren't infallible.

turns.speaker: Lord Rooker
turns.text: Last year about 15% of our power came through undersea cables from other countries. Why are we so reliant on them?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: They give us access to a bigger market, which keeps prices down, and let us sell spare wind power abroad. Weather differs between countries, so there's usually somewhere that can help.

turns.speaker: Lord Rooker
turns.text: And if our neighbours have the same weather and can't spare any?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: NESO doesn't count on getting their full output, and we make sure there's enough backup capacity in Britain to fill the gap.

turns.speaker: Lord Rooker
turns.text: Cables on the seabed are much harder to protect than land links on the continent. Has deliberate damage been taken care of?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Every source of power has a weak spot. Our job is to have enough variety that losing one cable or one big power station doesn't matter. The cables have been very reliable, but they aren't infallible.

turns.speaker: Lord Trees
turns.text: Does anyone check that imported power comes from low-carbon sources?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: I don't believe there's any requirement. Power traded on European markets doesn't come labelled with how it was made. It's not my area of expertise, though.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: If we lost the foreign cables at a time of peak demand, could we produce enough power ourselves?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: With no wind or sun and demand at its peak, there's some dependence on imports, but not total dependence. You can't protect against absolutely everything without making the system enormously expensive.

turns.speaker: Baroness McIntosh of Pickering
turns.text: Could new cables from the Netherlands and Belgium come ashore along the Thames and feed London directly?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: There's nothing in the regulations to stop it. Private developers choose where cables land, and I don't know whether it's technically possible.

chapters.title: What's really holding things up
chapters.takeaway: Ofgem says the biggest obstacle isn't its own rules but how slowly the grid is being built and projects connected to it.

turns.speaker: Earl Russell
turns.text: What regulations are still getting in the way of building storage and low-carbon power stations?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Nothing particular comes to mind. The main problem is the grid: building it and getting new projects connected. Our job is to make sure the grid companies get the money and build quickly, without us holding them up.

turns.speaker: Earl Russell
turns.text: And what's coming next on the grid?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Once the national energy plan is done, there'll be a follow-on plan for the high-voltage grid. We'll make sure the grid companies can raise the money to build what it says we need.
